lesson.title: Five Ways Real Populations Break the Rules
lesson.summary: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes a population that is not evolving, and the five assumptions required for that state to hold are, one by one, a list of the real forces that drive evolutionary change whenever they are violated.
lesson.body:
Recall that Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a kind of null hypothesis for a population: a mathematical snapshot of what allele and genotype frequencies would look like generation after generation if nothing were pushing the population to change. It is useful precisely because real populations essentially never meet it. To reach that idealized, non-evolving state, a population must satisfy five conditions at once. Each one, when it fails on its own, becomes a specific, nameable mechanism of evolutionary change, which is exactly why this list matters: it is also a preview of most of the rest of population genetics.

The five assumptions are these: no mutation occurring in the population, mating that is completely random with respect to genotype, no natural selection, meaning every genotype survives and reproduces equally well, a population size that is extremely large, ideally infinite, and no gene flow, meaning no individuals or gametes moving into or out of the population. Four of these map directly onto forces you will study individually in this unit. Mutation introduces new alleles. Non-random mating, including the special case of sexual selection, changes how genotypes combine. A small population size opens the door to genetic drift. Gene flow moves alleles between populations. The fifth, natural selection, is the force you likely already know best.

Why build a model out of assumptions that are almost never true in nature? Because science needs a baseline against which to measure deviation. Suppose a biologist samples a population of ground beetles and finds that one genotype at a particular gene is much rarer, or much more common, than the Hardy-Weinberg equations predict from the allele frequencies observed. That gap is a signal, not noise. It tells the biologist something specific is happening: perhaps a new mutation has appeared, perhaps beetles are mating non-randomly with respect to that gene, perhaps one genotype survives less often than the others, perhaps the population is small enough for chance alone to matter, or perhaps beetles are migrating in from a neighboring population. Figuring out which assumption is being violated, and by how much, is often the actual scientific work in a population genetics study.

One subtlety is worth flagging. The no mutation and no selection assumptions do not require that mutation or selection never happen anywhere, ever. They require that, within the timeframe and population being modeled, these forces are not measurably shifting allele frequencies. A population can sit in approximate Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a given gene across a few generations even though mutation is technically always occurring at some low background rate, simply because that rate is too slow to detect over a short window. The five assumptions describe the conditions under which change is negligible, and the rest of this unit is about what happens once any one of them stops being negligible.
